new_statements.quote: [2020, sect. 2.3] Lexemes in general consist of two or three syllables, sometimes they are monosyllabic and often they consist of more than three syllables (in particular inflected verbs). Stress is rarely marked and is not fixed. It is important as phrasal accent and moves towards the end of the word if clitic(s) is/are present. || [2000, fn. 5] Il nous est difficile d'être précis par rapport au problème de l'accent en zénaga. Les constatations faites pour le berbère semblent valables en général pour ce dialecte, notamment son caractère léger et son absence de fonction distinctive (S. Chaker, 1995: 98). Concernant la place de l'accent, cependant, nous sommes tentés de reprendre pour le zénaga ... celle formulée par J. Lanfry pour Ghadamès (1968: 325), qui oppose l'accentuation sur la 1ère syllabe pour l'impératif et l'aoriste (éknəf, yéknəf) à celle sur la 2e syllabe pour le prétérit (iknéf).
new_statements.translation: 2000 fn. 5: 'It is difficult for us to be precise about the problem of accent in Zenaga. The observations made for Berber seem generally valid for this dialect, notably its light character and its lack of distinctive function (Chaker 1995: 98). As for the place of the accent, however, we are tempted to adopt for Zenaga, not the Kabyle rule opposing nouns and verbs, but the one formulated by J. Lanfry for Ghadames (1968: 325), which opposes accent on the 1st syllable for the imperative and aorist (éknəf, yéknəf) to accent on the 2nd syllable for the preterite (iknéf).'

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked in (1) Taine-Cheikh 2020, 'Zenaga', Oxford Handbook of African Languages 530-542, HAL author ms; HAL cover page confirms the citation). extracted text per page: heading '2.3 Syllable structure' is on pdf p.4, and pdf p.5 lines 3-5 read exactly: 'Lexemes in general consist of two or three syllables, sometimes they are monosyllabic and often they consist of more than three syllables (in particular inflected verbs). Stress is rarely marked and is not fixed. It is important as phrasal accent and moves towards the end of the word if clitic(s) is/are present.' -- verbatim as quoted, immediately before '3 Morphology'. (2) Cohen & Taine-Cheikh 2000, BSL 95(1); HAL cover says pp. 269-3…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the principal describer, Zenaga word stress is weak (rarely perceptible), non-contrastive and has no fixed position; prominence functions mainly as a phrasal accent, shifting toward the end of the word when clitics attach. Tentative partial observations: in verbs, accent on the 1st syllable in imperative/aorist vs 2nd syllable in the preterite (2000, hedged 'nous sommes tentes'); accent 'seems to depend exclusively on syllable structure' (2008, Berber in Contact p. ~118); the author states (2025 fn. 2) that no exhaustive study of Zenaga accentuation exists.
new_statements.exceptions: Clitics pull the accent toward the end of the word (2020); genitive connector n is never accented and each noun of a genitive phrase tends to keep its own accent (2025); vowel length is independent of accent (2023 EB; 2000).
new_statements.domain_note: Author explicitly frames prominence as chiefly phrasal ('important as phrasal accent'); word+clitic group is the accentual unit; statements are impressionistic, not instrumental (the 1997 acoustic study measured vowels only).
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern Zenaga of south-west Mauritania (Trarza), Taine-Cheikh's data chiefly from an Idab Lahsen (Idābləḥsan) speaker (M. Ould Ahmedou Yahya); same language as zena1248, no separate dialect glottocode needed.

sources.note: Sect. 12 'The accent': no full comparison of Berber accent systems exists; aorist-initial vs perfective-second-syllable accent found in Libyan varieties and Tetserret (closely related to Zenaga, Lux 2013: 284ff); nothing specific on Zenaga accent.

sources.citation: Cohen, David & Catherine Taine-Cheikh. 2000. A propos du zenaga. Vocalisme et morphologie verbale en berbere. Bulletin de la Societe de Linguistique de Paris 95(1): 267-320. (HAL halshs-00460233)
sources.note: Fn. 5: hard to be precise about accent in Zenaga; it is light and non-distinctive as in Berber generally; for its place, authors are tempted to adopt Lanfry's Ghadames rule: 1st syllable in imperative and aorist (eknef, yeknef) vs 2nd syllable in preterite (iknef). Body text notes accent shift and vowel reduction under some suffixation; long accented vowels are longer.
